title: Building FLOW FIRE BODYCAM with AI — A Huge Leap in Gunplay & Visuals
author: Sweet-Chip6849
selftext:
I've been developing FLOW FIRE BODYCAM, an indie bodycam FPS built in Godot with AI agents, mainly Claude Opus and DeepSeek.

I don't write the code myself. I direct the development, test the game, make creative decisions, and decide what needs to change. The AI agents handle the programming and implementation.

The latest improvements have been a huge step forward.

One of our biggest challenges was making the weapons, arms, body, and camera move naturally together. Earlier versions had exaggerated camera movement when firing, so we went through multiple iterations to make the recoil feel more convincing.

We've also significantly improved image clarity, lighting adaptation, camera realism, and enemy reactions.

What's particularly interesting is that we've built our own testing tools that let the AI agents run the game, record gameplay, analyze movements, and compare results between versions. It's not just prompting once and hoping for the best — it's a continuous process of testing, finding problems, and refining the experience.

The video shows real gameplay from the current pre-alpha build. Development is moving quickly, and more improvements are already underway.

I'm documenting the progress as the game evolves.

For those developing games with AI, how are you testing and evaluating things like animation, gunplay, and the overall feel of movement?

replies.author: Sweet-Chip6849
replies.body:
Hey! Great question!

I'm not generating the weapon meshes entirely from scratch with AI. I'm using properly licensed base models from Sketchfab and having AI agents work with them in Blender and Godot.

For example, the Glock 19 uses a model by Rotuma, while the AK-47 is based on work by DuqueCD7.

Where AI really comes into play is everything around those assets: adapting the models, working with rigs and animations, improving hand placement, weapon handling, recoil, aiming, and how the weapon interacts with the player's body and camera.

Claude Opus and DeepSeek handle the programming and Blender automation, while I direct the development and evaluate the results in-game.

We've even built automated testing tools to record gameplay and measure how the weapons and camera move.

It's been a lot of experimentation, but the results are getting better with every iteration!

I'd be happy to exchange ideas about AI-assisted Blender workflows. Your project looks interesting too!

replies.author: Sweet-Chip6849
replies.body:
I actually love that idea!

I think there's a lot of potential for a community focused specifically on FPS games developed with AI.

It would be awesome to see developers sharing gameplay, experiments, weapon systems, animations, and actual development progress instead of just finished projects.

I'm documenting the evolution of FLOW FIRE BODYCAM as I build it, and I'd definitely be interested in being part of something like that!
